A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUB research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of misleading instructions, MUB benchmark results, fine-tuning experiments, and supplementary analyses, including Tables 1–23.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results on calibration, human-generated instructions, generative tasks, and video/audio inputs.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 retain the two-stage response comparison, GPT-4o-generated implicit instructions, benchmark difficulty selection, and mixed explicit/implicit LoRA fine-tuning. The expanded evaluations and explanations do not establish a changed core algorithm, architecture, or training objective.

E1.justification: The original nine image-benchmark evaluations remain. v2 adds free-response generation using MUB questions and Video-MME evaluation with video and audiovisual inputs (Appendices A.2.5–A.2.6). Image-embedded misleading watermarks and typo-noise scenarios also broaden the evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 expands quantitative instruction-generator comparisons to additional MLLMs and humans (Tables 13–14), and adds direct-warning and example-based defenses beyond the existing CoT comparison (Tables 24–25). Comparator membership also contracts in places: Yi-VL-34B is removed from the MMStar/AI2D comparison in Table 21.

E3.justification: Reported implicitness scoring changes from pairwise wins to numeric rubric ratings. New protocols include one/three/five-cue sampling, GPT-4o correctness judgments for 200 generative samples, and a 700-sample MR–consistency analysis. Table 9 is re-described as combining five instructions instead of randomly selecting one; its original MR values remain, so rerunning is not established.

E4.justification: v2 adds sampling-budget, prompt-position/repetition, watermark, typo, and flagged-deception tests, plus calibration and detailed task-level analyses. Figures 11–12 directly examine accuracy and consistency relationships with misleading rate. Existing masking, image-removal, option-order, and fine-tuning ablations are largely retained or reorganized.

E5.justification: Consistency estimation continues to use 20 responses. The new cue-sampling sweeps concern attack budgets, and ECE evaluates model calibration; neither introduces uncertainty intervals for experimental estimates. Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds calibration, generative, video/audio, defense, and task-breakdown results. Existing values also change: Table 2 revises MiniCPM-v-v2's low-difficulty implicit MR from 8.4% to 24.08%; its high-difficulty S5 result changes from 23.53% in v1 Table 18 to 2.53% in v2 Table 27. Table 1's original MR scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 retain the definitions of average consistency, transition-specific misleading rate, and normalized category proportions. No theorem or proof is added. The new implicitness rubric and calibration evaluation concern empirical metrics.

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain the misleading-rate evaluation, MUB construction, and mixed-instruction fine-tuning. v2 emphasizes preserving originally correct answers and correct-to-incorrect transitions, while retaining reverse-transition results. Its introduction elevates unsuccessful warning-based defenses to a key observation, replacing the earlier emphasis on confidence and unknown responses.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting fine-tuning to calibration and uncertainty awareness, and uses typo/flagged-deception probes to examine explanations based solely on instruction-following. A new Limitations section explicitly qualifies the applicability of deliberately misleading, worst-case prompts to everyday interactions. These extend v1's robustness and overconfidence discussion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies training-data selection from groups misleading 7, 8, 10, or 11 models, documents human annotation, and adds scoring and fine-tuning prompt examples. It changes the advertised code repository. Conversely, v1's dataset-by-level count table and checkpoint/JSON release pledge disappear; core training hyperparameters and hardware descriptions remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on video models/benchmarks, calibration, and medical/driving applications, including Cheng et al., Fu et al., Guo et al., and Arora et al. Several earlier references, including Bai et al.'s hallucination survey, disappear. The central positioning relative to MAD-Bench, AVIBench, and MMR remains similar.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Benchmark analyses and related work move into reorganized appendices, the main experimental narrative concentrates on two research questions, and Appendix A.2 gains six subsections. New acknowledgements and limitations accompany substantial restructuring and expanded explanations.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column document. Figure 3 expands from seven displayed models to twelve; Tables 1–2 gain accuracy columns; masking tables merge; and fine-tuning panels are redistributed. Numerous analysis tables and correlation/prompt figures are added, while the source-count table and one benchmark-distribution panel are removed.

improvement.justification: The new defense comparisons, generative/video tests, and calibration and MR–consistency analyses strengthen validation beyond v1's narrower evidence. The explicit real-world limitation also improves qualification. However, reporting problems limit the gain: v2 claims negligible position effects despite Table 11 reporting 57.17% versus 79.38% MR for different positions, and revised entries in Tables 2 and 27 retain inconsistent averages. The added evidence is useful, but these problems prevent a substantial overall improvement.
